lessons.title: Soil Testing and Interpretation for Tropical Fruits
lessons.body: Soil testing is the first step to growing healthy tropical fruit trees. Without a soil test, you are guessing what your soil needs. In Africa, you can get a soil test done at your local agricultural extension office or a private lab for about $20 to $50. Collect soil samples from 10 to 15 spots in your orchard, digging 15 cm deep for each sample. Mix them in a clean bucket, then take about 500 grams of the mixed soil to the lab. The lab will test for pH, organic matter, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium, magnesium, and micronutrients like zinc and boron. For most tropical fruits, the ideal soil pH is between 5.5 and 6.5. If your pH is below 5.0, add agricultural lime at 2 to 4 tonnes per hectare. If above 7.0, add elemental sulfur or gypsum. The lab report will give you levels in parts per million (ppm) or meq/100g. For example, phosphorus should be 10-20 ppm, potassium 100-200 ppm. If your levels are low, you need to add fertilizers. If high, avoid adding more. Always test before planting and then every 2-3 years. Many farmers skip testing and waste money on fertilizers they don't need. A simple pH test kit costs $10 and can be done at home. But for full nutrient analysis, use a lab. Remember: different fruits have different needs. Avocado prefers pH 5.5-6.5, mango 5.5-7.0, citrus 5.5-6.5. So test your soil and adjust accordingly.

lessons.title: Organic Matter and Compost Production
lessons.body: Organic matter is the life of your soil. It holds water, feeds beneficial microbes, and releases nutrients slowly. In tropical Africa, you can make compost from crop residues, animal manure, kitchen waste, and grass clippings. A simple compost pile should be 1 meter high and 1.5 meters wide. Layer dry materials (like maize stalks, dry leaves) with green materials (like fresh grass, vegetable scraps) and manure. Aim for a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 25:1 to 30:1. If too dry, add water; if too wet, add dry material. Turn the pile every 2 weeks to add oxygen. In 6 to 8 weeks, you will have dark, crumbly compost that smells like earth. Apply 5 to 10 tonnes per hectare per year, or about 2 to 4 kg per tree, spread around the drip line. You can also make compost tea: soak 1 kg of compost in 10 liters of water for 3 days, then strain and spray on leaves or soil. Another option is vermicompost using earthworms. Use a bin with bedding like shredded paper, add 1 kg of worms per square meter, and feed them kitchen scraps. Worm castings are rich in nutrients. In dry areas, mulch with organic matter to conserve moisture. Never burn crop residues; instead, compost them. This saves money on fertilizers and improves soil health. Start a compost pile today using materials you already have.

lessons.title: Essential Nutrients and Deficiency Symptoms
lessons.body: Plants need 16 essential nutrients. The big three are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Nitrogen makes leaves green and promotes growth. Deficiency shows as yellowing of older leaves first. Add urea or manure. Phosphorus helps roots and flowers. Deficiency causes purple leaves and poor fruiting. Add rock phosphate or bone meal. Potassium strengthens stems and fruit quality. Deficiency shows as yellow or brown edges on older leaves. Add wood ash or potassium sulfate. Secondary nutrients are calcium, magnesium, and sulfur. Calcium deficiency causes blossom end rot in fruits like mango and avocado. Add lime or gypsum. Magnesium deficiency shows as yellowing between veins on older leaves. Add Epsom salts (magnesium sulfate) at 1 tablespoon per liter of water as a foliar spray. Micronutrients include zinc, boron, iron, manganese, and copper. Zinc deficiency causes small, mottled leaves. Spray zinc sulfate at 0.5%. Boron deficiency causes cracked fruits and hollow stems. Apply borax at 10-20 kg per hectare. Iron deficiency shows as yellow leaves with green veins. Lower pH or add chelated iron. In Africa, sandy soils often lack nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, while acidic soils may lack calcium and magnesium. Always diagnose before treating. A soil test and leaf analysis (send leaves to a lab) will confirm. Over-fertilizing can also cause problems, like burning roots or killing microbes. So apply only what is needed.

lessons.title: Fertilizer Types and Application Methods
lessons.body: Fertilizers come in two main types: organic and inorganic. Organic fertilizers include manure, compost, and bone meal. They release nutrients slowly and improve soil structure. Inorganic fertilizers are concentrated and fast-acting. Common ones are urea (46-0-0), triple superphosphate (0-46-0), and potassium chloride (0-0-60). You can also buy blended fertilizers like NPK 20-10-10. For tropical fruits, apply fertilizers based on soil test results. A general recommendation for a mature mango tree is 1 kg of NPK 12-12-17 per year, split into two applications. For young trees, use 100-200 grams per year. Apply fertilizer in a ring around the tree at the drip line, not touching the trunk. Water after applying. For phosphorus, incorporate it into the soil before planting because it moves slowly. For nitrogen and potassium, split applications during the rainy season. Foliar sprays are good for quick correction of micronutrient deficiencies. Use a knapsack sprayer with a fine mist. Always wear gloves and a mask when handling fertilizers. Store them in a dry place. Organic options like poultry manure should be composted first to avoid burning plants. In Africa, you can make your own fertilizer by mixing 1 part urine (diluted 1:10 with water) with compost. This provides nitrogen. Remember: more fertilizer is not always better. Follow the label and soil test.

lessons.title: Mulching and Soil Moisture Conservation
lessons.body: Mulching is covering the soil around your fruit trees with organic or inorganic material. It conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and regulates soil temperature. In tropical Africa, use dry grass, straw, banana leaves, or crop residues. Spread a layer 5 to 10 cm thick around the tree, keeping it 10 cm away from the trunk to prevent rot. Do not use fresh grass or leaves that may contain seeds or diseases. For dry areas, mulch can reduce water evaporation by up to 70%. You can also use plastic mulch (black or silver) for vegetable crops, but for fruit trees, organic mulch is better because it adds nutrients as it decomposes. Another method is living mulch: plant cover crops like cowpea or lablab between trees. They fix nitrogen and cover the soil. But avoid plants that compete for water and nutrients. In addition to mulching, dig basins or swales to catch rainwater. A simple basin around each tree, 1 meter wide and 15 cm deep, can hold water. You can also use drip irrigation with mulch to save water. In very dry regions, use stone mulch or gravel around the base. Never leave soil bare. Mulch also prevents soil erosion from heavy rains. Reapply mulch every 6 months as it breaks down. This is one of the cheapest and most effective ways to keep your fruit trees healthy.

lessons.title: Practical: Developing a Fertilizer Program
lessons.body: Now you will create a fertilizer program for your own fruit orchard. First, get a soil test. If you cannot afford a lab, use a home test kit for pH and NPK. Next, identify your fruit trees and their age. For example, a 2-year-old avocado tree needs different amounts than a 10-year-old mango. Write down the recommended nutrients from your soil test. If your soil is low in nitrogen, you need to add urea or manure. If low in phosphorus, add triple superphosphate. If low in potassium, add potassium sulfate. Then decide on fertilizer types: organic, inorganic, or a mix. For a small farm, compost and manure are cheap. For larger farms, blended NPK may be easier. Calculate the amount per tree. For a mature citrus tree, a common program is 500 g of NPK 13-13-13 in early spring, then 500 g of urea in late spring, and 500 g of potassium sulfate in summer. Split applications to avoid leaching. Apply in a ring at the drip line. Water well. Keep a calendar: mark when to apply, what to apply, and how much. Also include foliar sprays for micronutrients every 2 months. Monitor your trees for deficiency symptoms and adjust. After one year, take a leaf sample to see if your program worked. Record everything in a notebook. This practical exercise will save you money and increase your harvest. Share your program with other farmers.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for most tropical fruit trees?
quiz.explanation: Most tropical fruits like avocado, mango, and citrus grow best in slightly acidic soil with pH 5.5-6.5.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig when collecting soil samples for testing?
quiz.explanation: A depth of 15 cm is standard for soil sampling as it represents the root zone for most fruit trees.

quiz.q: What is the first symptom of nitrogen deficiency in plants?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile, so the plant moves it from older leaves to new growth, causing older leaves to yellow first.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes blossom end rot in fruits?
quiz.explanation: Calcium is essential for cell wall strength, and deficiency leads to blossom end rot in fruits like mango and avocado.

quiz.q: What is the ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for compost?
quiz.explanation: A C:N ratio of 25:1 to 30:1 provides the best conditions for microbial decomposition in compost.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 2 weeks adds oxygen and speeds up decomposition without over-managing.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is a good source of phosphorus?
quiz.explanation: Triple superphosphate is a concentrated phosphorus fertilizer (0-46-0).

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of compost per tree per year?
quiz.explanation: Applying 2-4 kg of compost per tree per year improves soil health without over-fertilizing.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes small, mottled leaves?
quiz.explanation: Zinc deficiency typically causes small, mottled leaves and shortened internodes.

quiz.q: What is the best way to apply phosphorus fertilizer?
options: B) Incorporate into soil before planting
D) Mix with water and pour
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus moves slowly in soil, so it should be incorporated into the root zone before planting.

quiz.q: Which mulch material is best for fruit trees?
quiz.explanation: Dry grass or straw is organic, adds nutrients, and does not contain seeds or diseases like fresh grass.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be around fruit trees?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer conserves moisture and suppresses weeds without suffocating roots.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching?
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces water evaporation from the soil surface by up to 70%.

quiz.q: Which of these is a secondary nutrient?
quiz.explanation: Calcium, magnesium, and sulfur are secondary nutrients needed in moderate amounts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of lime if soil pH is below 5.0?
quiz.explanation: To raise pH significantly, apply 2-4 tonnes of agricultural lime per hectare.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is a good source of nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Urea is 46% nitrogen, one of the highest concentrations available.

quiz.q: What is compost tea?
options: B) Soaking compost in water to extract nutrients
quiz.explanation: Compost tea is made by soaking compost in water, then using the liquid as a foliar feed or soil drench.

quiz.q: Which method conserves soil moisture in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: Mulching covers the soil, reducing evaporation and keeping moisture available to roots.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of potassium deficiency?
options: C) Brown or yellow edges on older leaves
D) Green veins on yellow leaves
quiz.explanation: Potassium deficiency often shows as scorched or yellowed leaf margins on older leaves.

quiz.q: How often should you test your soil?
quiz.explanation: Soil testing every 2-3 years helps monitor nutrient levels and adjust fertilizer programs.

quiz.q: Which of these is an organic fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Compost is made from decomposed organic matter and is a natural fertilizer.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a foliar spray?
options: B) To quickly correct nutrient deficiencies
quiz.explanation: Foliar sprays deliver nutrients directly to leaves for rapid absorption and quick correction of deficiencies.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is important for root development?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus promotes root growth, flowering, and fruiting.

quiz.q: What is a living mulch?
options: B) Cover crops planted between trees
quiz.explanation: Living mulch uses cover crops like cowpea to cover soil, fix nitrogen, and reduce erosion.

quiz.q: How much water can mulch save?
quiz.explanation: Mulch can reduce evaporation by up to 70%, significantly conserving water.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of boron for deficiency correction?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10-20 kg of borax per hectare to correct boron deficiency, but avoid over-application.

quiz.q: Which fruit tree prefers a slightly acidic soil pH of 5.5-6.5?
quiz.explanation: Avocado grows best in slightly acidic soil with pH between 5.5 and 6.5.

quiz.q: What is a key step in developing a fertilizer program?
quiz.explanation: A soil test provides the baseline data needed to determine which nutrients to apply and how much.

quiz.q: Which of these is a micronutrient?
quiz.explanation: Zinc is a micronutrient needed in small amounts for healthy growth.

quiz.q: What should you do after applying fertilizer?
options: A) Leave it on the surface
quiz.explanation: Watering after fertilizer application helps dissolve nutrients and move them into the root zone.
